title: Fish-shaped palette

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Rogers Fund, 1935
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A flat, smooth gray-green stone cut into the simple shape of a fish, wider than it is tall, with a rounded body and a tail at one end.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, date, medium, period, dimensions, tags (Fish), public-domain flag, credit line and image URLs read from the record

context: A stone palette from Predynastic Egypt, made around 3300–3100 BCE and carved in the shape of a fish. It is about 23.5 cm wide and 11.9 cm high. Palettes of this kind are usually thought to have been used for grinding pigments.

descriptions.k: This is a fish made of stone. It has a round body and a tail. It is flat and smooth. It was made more than five thousand years ago. Can you find which end is the head?
descriptions.g12: An Egyptian carver shaped this gray-green stone into a fish more than 5,000 years ago. It is flat, with a curved body and a tail. Palettes like this were probably used to grind colors. What parts of a fish can you find, even though it is so simple?
descriptions.g35: This palette was carved from greywacke, a hard gray-green stone, in the shape of a fish. It was made in Egypt over 5,000 years ago, when people lived beside the Nile and fish were part of daily life. Palettes like this were probably used to grind pigments. Follow the outline from the head to the tail. How does such a simple shape still say "fish"?
descriptions.g68: Made around 3300–3100 BCE, this palette is only about 23.5 cm wide, yet it captures a fish with a single, clean contour. The shape probably served a practical purpose for grinding pigments, but the choice of an animal suggests the maker cared about more than function. Because the stone is smooth and unpainted, we notice outline and proportion first. What might this simple form tell us about how early Egyptian artists saw the Nile and its creatures?
descriptions.g910: This Naqada III palette reduces a fish to its essentials: a long, tapering body and a clear tail in a single thin slab of greywacke. The effect depends on contour and proportion rather than surface detail. Palettes are generally associated with grinding mineral pigments, and animal shapes may have carried symbolic or status meanings, though scholars remain cautious. How does the object blend practical form and imagery, and what does its restraint communicate?
descriptions.g1112: The fish palette shows how Predynastic craftsmen could invest a utilitarian slab of stone with subtle sculptural intelligence. Silhouette serves as both representation and structure, and the hardness of the greywacke suggests deliberate labor and value. Archaeologists commonly link such palettes to the preparation of pigments, yet their forms, which include many animals, point to ritual or social functions that remain debated. Because the object has no inscription, its meaning must be argued from material, form, and comparison rather than assumed.

teacherNote.context: A Predynastic palette in fish form, generally interpreted as a tool for grinding pigments. Its simplicity makes it a good object for discussing silhouette and abstraction.
directions: Have students draw a fish using only an outline and compare which details they needed.
Ask students to argue what this palette's purpose might have been using only visible evidence and the context line.
Pair with the guinea fowl palette to compare two animal silhouettes from the same culture.
